To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
locomotion modulates the activity of different interneuron populations in a context dependent manner.

locomotion increases activity in all interneuron subtypes and excitatory neurons during visual stimulation, but that the proportion of responsive cells varies across subtypes and is dependent on the behavioral context.
locomotion modulates the activity of VIP, SST and PV interneurons during light, but not darkness, with context dependent locomotion responses in each cell type.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the thalamus in sensory perception and cognition, with a special focus on the role of the reticular nucleus in regulating the flow of sensory information from the thalamus to the cortex.
the neural mechanisms underlying the control of behavior by sensory stimuli and how these mechanisms are modulated by internal states.
the role of inhibition in the visual cortex, with the goal of understanding the neural mechanisms that underlie the control of sensory responses in behavior
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
“The present study demonstrates that locomotion modulates inhibitory interneurons differently, depending on the context.
locomotion has differential effects on VIP, PV and SST interneurons, depending on the context (light/dark) and that these differential effects are not consistent across cell types.
the behavioral modulation of inhibition is cell type and context dependent in the visual cortex.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the modulation of inhibition by locomotion is not only cell type specific but also context dependent.

locomotion is not the only factor that modulates neuronal activity in the cortex, but rather that locomotion modulates the activity of different cell types in different behavioral contexts, and that these effects can be context dependent.
locomotion modulates the response of inhibitory neurons in a cell type and stimulus dependent manner.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the behavioral state modulation of cortical responses is context dependent and that the circuit mechanism for behavioral state modulation of sensory responses is not the same for all cell types in the cortex.
the modulation of neuronal activity in the cortex by locomotion is cell type specific and depends on the behavioral context.
the modulation of neuronal responses by locomotion is not uniform across cortical cell types and is context dependent.
